Introducing computer-use agents, improved clinical answers, and new healthcare plugins that work across healthcare software to get real work done.

Healthcare teams need to piece together information from the EHR, hospital policies, scheduling systems, and payer portals to deliver care and manage operations. With ChatGPT for Healthcare, we’re bringing the tools teams already use and the medical evidence they need into one platform to help them spend less time navigating systems and more time caring for patients.

Today, we’re sharingadvances in computer-use agents⁠, which lets AI agents carry out multi-step work across existing healthcare software. We’re also improving trusted clinical search, which finds, evaluates, and cites medical evidence, and introducing more than 20 new plugins to the healthcare plugin ecosystem.

Together, these capabilities help healthcare teams find the information they need, make decisions grounded in medical evidence, and carry out next steps across the systems they already use.

Organizations often need to move information between disconnected systems to prepare documentation, coordinate care, and complete administrative tasks. Computer-use agents can help with these steps by navigating the software that teams already use: reading screens, clicking, typing, and moving between applications.

Today, we’re sharing advances in computer-use agents for healthcare, including more capable, safe, and affordable models for clinical and administrative workflows, and access controls and audit logs for secure deployments. We’re also sharing our work with healthcare organizations that are deploying agents, including Abridge, Ambience, Cigna Healthcare, and CVS Health, to process referrals, move documents between systems, and bring together the information care teams need. In the demo below, a clinician uses Voice in the ChatGPT app to ask for help following up on an MRI request. The agent reviews the chart and drafts an order and patient reply for review.

Healthcare organizations can start with a workflow that spans existing applications, set which applications agents can access, and establish clear controls for which steps require human review. To support HIPAA-compliant workflows involving protected health information, organizations must use eligible services covered by their BAA with OpenAI, apply required security and retention settings, and extend protections to connected systems. Content shared with ChatGPT for Healthcare is not used to train models.

Read more about our computer use research, customer stories, and demonstrations inAdvancing computer-use agents for healthcare teams⁠.

We’re improving trusted clinical search in ChatGPT for Healthcare and ChatGPT for Clinicians, including how ChatGPT finds, evaluates, and cites medical evidence. These updates help clinicians connect relevant evidence to clinical questions and translate it into practical next steps, with citations they can inspect.

To measure the impact of these updates, in a blind evaluation, physicians reviewed responses to real-world clinical questions across multiple specialties, including multi-turn conversations. In over 1300 reviews, physicians rated the updated experience more highly across all eight dimensions evaluated, including factual correctness, safety, actionability, and source authoritativeness.

We’re expanding our healthcare plugin ecosystem with more than 20 new healthcare plugins from leading companies across clinical care, care coordination, and business operations. All of these are available today in ChatGPT for Healthcare, including throughChartGPT, which brings ChatGPT into the EHR workflow⁠.

These plugins let teams bring more of their work into the same conversation: reviewing patient records and hospital protocols, preparing prescriptions for clinician review, coordinating patient outreach, checking insurance eligibility, and analyzing healthcare costs and operational performance.

articles.title: Alibaba Releases Qwen4-Max: 2.4T MoE, 71B Active, 1M Context
articles.content: Alibaba’s Qwen team has released Qwen4-Max, the first model of its Qwen4 generation. Qwen4-Max is a proprietary sparse MoE model with a 2.4T-parameter backbone and 71B parameters active per token. It accepts text, images and video, and supports a 1M-token context window. Alibaba also cut API prices and reports a 62% drop in average cost per task. TL;DR Size: 2.4T backbone parameters, 71B active per token, plus 328B N-gram Embedding parameters. 1M context, 393K max output tokens. Runs on: Hosted only: QwenCloud API, Token Plan, Qwen Studio, QwenWork and Qoder. No open weights, so no self-hosting or quantized builds. Performance: A large jump over Qwen3.8-Max. Competitive with frontier models on agentic work, behind on hard coding and vision. Best: HLAB-Vals-1.1 (legal agent work): 21.3, versus 11.7 for Kimi K3.1, the next-best model. What is Qwen4-Max? Qwen4-Max is a multimodal MoE language model from Alibaba, built for long-horizon professional work. A Token Plan-only preview opened this month only. How does the Qwen4-Max architecture work? Qwen4 upgrades the sparse MoE design in 3 places: attention, residual connections and embeddings. GDN + Qwen Sparse Attention (QSA): Each QSA layer pairs with 3 Gated DeltaNet layers. These compress history into fixed-size states. QSA then uses a lightweight indexer to pick relevant context at micro-block granularity. This lowers attention and indexing cost on long sequences. Gated Residual (GR): 4 parallel residual branches use dynamic read and write gates. The aim is stronger information flow and better training stability. N-gram Embedding: 328B extra parameters provide lookups of local token patterns at layer 2. This adds capacity with little extra compute. Alibaba reports no loss spikes across the 2.4T-scale pre-training run. On in-house tests, Qwen4-Max-Base shows 5 to 13% lower bits per byte than Qwen3.8-Max-Base. It does this while activating 25% fewer parameters. How does Qwen4-Max perform on benchmarks? Alibaba’s comparison chart covers 16 benchmarks. Rivals are Qwen3.8-Max-0902, Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-6.1 Sol, GPT-6 Astra and Kimi K3.1. Several scores are cited from third-party leaderboards. None were independently reproduced at launch. Qwen4-Max ranks first on 4 of 16 benchmarks: HLAB-Vals-1.1 (legal agents): 21.3, versus 11.7 for Kimi K3.1 and 9.2 for Opus 5.5. Agents’ Last Exam v1.1: 46.7, versus 43.4 for Opus 5.5 and Kimi K3.1. BioMysteryBench: 85.0, versus 84.4 for GPT-6.1 Sol. DeepSWE v1.1: 75.7, versus 75.5 for Kimi K3.1. Claude Opus 5.5 leads 7 of the 16 charts. Qwen4-Max trails most clearly on coding and vision: ProgramBench: 31.5 versus 65.0 for Opus 5.5. Terminal-Bench 4.0: 48.5 versus 67.2 for Kimi K3.1. Chartography: 54.2 versus 71.1 for GPT-6 Astra. Humanity’s Last Exam: 51.7 versus 59.8 for Opus 5.5. On Alibaba’s own Work360 benchmark, Qwen4-Max scores 52.69, up from 47.74 for Qwen3.8-Max. Work360 spans 26 top-level domains and 721 specialized fields. && Why is Qwen4-Max cheaper to run? Two things stack: fewer tokens and lower prices. On Work360, token use drops about 24% at Xhigh effort and 35% at High effort. On Terminal-Bench 4.0, the drops are about 48% and 49%. Average Work360 cost per task falls from $4.43 to $1.67, a 62% cut. List prices fell too. Input is $1.50 per million tokens, down from $2 for Qwen3.8-Max. Output is $4.50, down from $6. Implicit cache reads drop 70%, from $0.25 to $0.075. How can developers use Qwen4-Max? The model ID is qwen4-max on QwenCloud. The API works with OpenAI-compatible and Anthropic-compatible clients. Supported features include function calling, structured outputs, context caching, batch processing, web search and fine-tuning. The default rate limit is 5,000,000 tokens per minute. Thinking mode is toggled with enable_thinking. Subscription access runs through the Token Plan. Key Takeaways 2.4T MoE backbone, only 71B active per token. New QSA attention, Gated Residuals and 328B N-gram Embeddings. First on 4 of 16 charted benchmarks, led by HLAB-Vals-1.1 at 21.3. $1.50/$4.50 per million tokens, cached input down 70%. Weak spots: ProgramBench (31.5) and Terminal-Bench 4.0 (48.5). Check out the official Qwen4-Max blog, the QwenCloud model page and the Token Plan pricing page. articles.summary: Alibaba가 텍스트·이미지·비디오를 처리하고 100만 토큰 문맥을 지원하는 Qwen4-Max를 공개했다고 보도됐다. 이 모델은 2.4조 파라미터 규모의 MoE 본체에서 토큰당 710억 파라미터를 활성화하며, Gated DeltaNet과 희소 어텐션, 게이트형 잔차 연결 및 별도의 N-gram 임베딩을 결합한다. Alibaba는 API 가격 인하와 함께 작업당 평균 비용이 62% 감소했다고 보고했지만, 이는 회사 측 수치다. 가중치는 공개되지 않아 자체 호스팅은 불가능하며, 장기 에이전트 업무에 경쟁력을 보이는 반면 고난도 코딩과 비전에서는 한계가 있다는 평가다.

articles.title: LG AI연구원, ‘K-엑사원 2.5’ API 전격 무료 개방…8주 만에 AI 성능 70%↑, 글로벌 프런티어 AI 정조준
articles.content:
LG AI연구원이 독자 개발한 인공지능(AI) 파운데이션 모델의 종합 성능을 단 8주 만에 70% 이상 끌어올리며 글로벌 프런티어 AI 경쟁에 속도를 내고 있다.

특히, AI가 스스로 계획을 수립하고 외부 도구를 활용해 업무를 수행하는 에이전틱 AI 분야에서 중국의 딥시크와 GLM 등 글로벌 오픈 웨이트 모델에 근접하거나 일부 성능을 앞서는 결과를 확보했다. LG AI연구원은 개선된 모델의 응용프로그램 인터페이스(API)를 전면 무료로 개방해 실제 서비스 환경에서 기술 검증을 확대한다.

LG AI연구원은 9일, 성능을 개선한 ‘K-엑사원 2.5(K-EXAONE 2.5)’를 전격 공개하고, 개발자와 기업, 연구기관 등이 무료로 활용할 수 있도록 API 서비스를 제공한다고 밝혔다. K-엑사원 2.5는 지난 8월 공개한 독자 AI 파운데이션 모델 2차수 버전에 추가 학습을 적용한 기술 검증 모델이다.

LG AI연구원은 새로운 3차수 모델 개발에 앞서 기존 모델의 학습 방법론을 고도화하고, 이를 통해 성능을 얼마나 개선할 수 있는지 확인하는 데 집중했다. 그 결과 자체 측정한 24개 평가 지표의 종합 성능이 8월 공개 모델보다 70% 이상 향상된 것으로 나타났다. 이번 성과는 데이터 품질과 학습 방법론의 개선을 통해 기존 모델의 성능을 단기간에 끌어올릴 수 있다는 가능성을 확인했다는 점에서 의미가 있다.

특히 에이전틱 AI의 실제 업무 수행 능력을 평가하는 주요 벤치마크에서 중국의 딥시크(DeepSeek) V4.1 Flash와 지엘엠(GLM) 5.3(max) 등 글로벌 프런티어급 오픈 웨이트 모델과 경쟁 가능한 결과를 기록했다.

LG AI연구원이 공개한 평가 결과에 따르면, 서비스형 소프트웨어(SaaS) 도구를 이용한 업무 자동화 능력을 측정하는 ‘오토메이션 벤치(AutomationBench)’에서 K-엑사원 2.5는 74.6점을 기록했다. 딥시크의 74.9점과 거의 비슷한 수준이며, GLM의 71.6점보다 3.0점 높았다.

업무 환경에서 AI 에이전트의 문제 해결 능력을 평가하는 ‘클로 이밸(Claw-Eval)’에서는 77.3점을 얻었다. 딥시크의 75.8점보다 1.5점 높았으며, GLM의 77.6점과는 0.3점 차이를 보였다.

웹을 탐색해 필요한 정보를 찾아내는 능력을 측정하는 ‘브라우즈컴프(BrowseComp)’에서는 78.0점을 기록했다. 딥시크의 75.8점을 2.2점 앞섰으며, GLM의 79.0점과는 1.0점 차이를 나타냈다. 소프트웨어 개발과 코드 수정 능력을 평가하는 ‘SWE-벤치 프로(SWE-Bench Pro)’에서는 59.2점을 기록해 딥시크의 58.4점보다 0.8점 높았지만, GLM의 64.0점에는 미치지 못했다.

공개된 네 가지 지표를 종합하면 K-엑사원 2.5는 딥시크보다 세 개 항목에서 높은 점수를 기록했으며, GLM과 비교해서는 한 개 항목에서 앞섰다. 이는 특정 에이전틱 AI 작업에서 글로벌 모델과 경쟁할 수 있는 성능을 확보했음을 보여준다.

다만 이번 결과는 LG AI연구원이 오픈 데이터셋을 활용해 자체 측정한 수치로, 독립적인 제3자 평가 결과는 아니다. 또한 70% 이상의 성능 향상은 24개 평가 지표를 종합한 내부 분석 결과이며, 공개된 네 가지 벤치마크에서 각각 70% 이상 개선됐다는 의미는 아니다.

김이른 LG AI연구원 엑사원랩장은 “내부 분석 결과 24개 평가 지표를 종합한 성능은 8월 공개 모델 대비 70% 이상 향상된 것을 확인했다”며 “이번 기술 검증 모델을 통해 빠르게 변하는 글로벌 벤치마크 환경에 대응할 핵심 학습 기술을 자체 확보했고, 프런티어급 성능을 구현할 기반을 마련했다”고 설명했다.

LG AI연구원은 이번 성능 개선을 실제 서비스 환경에서도 검증하기 위해 K-엑사원 2.5 API를 전면 무료로 개방했다. 개발자와 스타트업, 기업, 연구기관 등 누구나 공식 개발자 플랫폼에서 API 키를 발급받으면 별도 이용 비용 없이 모델을 서비스 개발과 연구에 활용할 수 있다.

공식 API 문서와 이용 안내는 엑사원 개발자 플랫폼(다운)에서 확인할 수 있다. 이번 무료 개방은 자체 벤치마크에서 확인한 성능을 실제 개발 환경으로 확장한다는 점에서 주목된다. 다양한 개발자와 기업이 모델을 직접 활용하면 업무 자동화와 정보 검색, 소프트웨어 개발 등 실제 응용 분야에서 모델의 활용 가능성과 개선 과제를 확인할 수 있기 때문이다.

AI 추론 인프라의 효율성과 서비스 확장성을 높이기 위한 엔비디아(NVIDIA)와의 기술 협력도 추진한다. LG AI연구원은 엔비디아의 AI 추론 인프라 최적화 기술인 ‘다이나모(Dynamo)’ 적용을 검토하고 있다. 엔비디아는 앞서 K-엑사원에 맞춘 다이나모 활용 가이드를 공개한 바 있다.

다이나모는 대규모 AI 모델의 추론 요청을 효율적으로 처리하기 위한 기술로, AI 서비스 운영 과정에서 연산 자원 활용과 처리 효율을 개선하는 데 활용할 수 있다. LG AI연구원은 이를 통해 향후 모델의 실제 서비스 적용과 운영 규모 확대에 필요한 기술적 기반을 강화한다는 구상이다.

LG AI연구원은 이번 기술 검증 결과를 차기 독자 AI 파운데이션 모델 개발에도 반영할 계획이다. 데이터 품질 개선과 사후 학습, 강화 학습 등 K-엑사원 2.5에서 검증한 독자 학습 기술을 3차수 모델에 적용하고, 2027년 1월까지 글로벌 프런티어급 성능을 갖춘 엑사원 모델을 완성한다는 목표다.

임우형 LG AI연구원 공동 연구원장은 “현재 3차수 모델 개발에 역량을 모으고 있으며, 이번 API 공개로 더 많은 개발자와 기업이 달라진 성능을 직접 체감하길 기대한다”며 “내년 1월까지 프런티어급 성능의 엑사원 모델을 완성하는 데 집중하겠다”고 강조했다.

이번 발표는 국내 AI 파운데이션 모델 개발 경쟁이 단순한 모델 공개를 넘어 학습 효율 개선과 실사용 성능 검증으로 확대되고 있음을 보여준다. 특히 에이전틱 AI가 기업의 업무 자동화와 소프트웨어 개발 등으로 확산되면서 모델의 지식 처리 능력뿐 아니라 도구 활용과 복합 작업 수행 능력이 중요한 평가 기준으로 부상하고 있다.

LG AI연구원이 제시한 8주간의 성능 개선 성과 역시 이러한 기술 경쟁의 변화를 반영한다. 앞으로 외부 평가와 실제 서비스 환경에서 성능 개선 효과가 얼마나 재현되는지가 중요한 검증 과제가 될 전망이다.

특히 K-엑사원 2.5의 무료 API 개방은 국내 개발자와 기업이 국산 AI 모델을 직접 평가하고 응용 서비스를 개발할 수 있는 기회를 확대한다는 점에서 의미가 있다. 향후 실제 이용 과정에서 확인되는 성능과 차기 모델의 기술적 완성도가 국내 AI 생태계의 경쟁력 강화로 이어질 수 있을지 주목된다.
articles.summary: LG AI연구원이 추가 학습으로 개선한 K-엑사원 2.5를 공개하고 개발자·기업·연구기관에 API를 무료로 제공한다고 밝혔다. 자체 평가에서 AutomationBench 74.6점, BrowseComp 78.0점, SWE-Bench Pro 59.2점을 기록해 일부 에이전트 작업에서 비교 대상 DeepSeek·GLM 모델과 근접하거나 앞서는 결과를 제시했다. 8주간 70% 이상 개선됐다는 수치는 24개 지표를 종합한 내부 분석으로, 개별 벤치마크마다 같은 폭으로 향상됐다는 의미는 아니다. 독립적인 검증은 제시되지 않았지만, 국내 개발자가 실제 서비스에서 모델을 시험할 비용 장벽을 낮춘다는 의미가 있다.

articles.title: Safety
articles.content:
November 16, 2026

We have signed agreements with four independent assessors—Apollo Research, METR, Transluce, and Goodfire—for our first phase of embedded assessments. As AI capabilities advance rapidly and the potential risks grow, public reporting from independent assessments can give people a clearer view of how labs are evaluating and managing those risks.

Embedded assessments give independent experts deep access to a lab’s internal models and systems to assess model alignment and the effectiveness of safeguards over an extended period of time, especially where relevant to our safety cases. Based on what each evaluation needs, assessors receive access to some of the same internal resources our researchers use, including model checkpoints, source code, training and evaluation data, monitoring systems, technical documentation, and discussions with the researchers and engineers responsible for the work. This access gives assessors the evidence and context to pursue independent evaluations and uncover failures we may not have anticipated.

Our initial assessments focus on alignment and safeguards for models during training and internal use, complementing oursafety cases. They build on ourpriorities and principles for third party assessmentsand years of work withthird party evaluators, including a recent pilot assessment ofour internal monitoring systems⁠(opens in a new window)with deep internal access and an investigation ofthe Hugging Face incident⁠(opens in a new window). We’ll use what we learn to deepen our work with independent experts in the coming months. These efforts also support our commitments under the White House Accord on Super Intelligence, where we agreed to independent assessments of our safety controls. These collaborations can contribute to stronger shared standards for independent assessment and public transparency across the industry.

In this pilot assessment,Apollo Research⁠(opens in a new window)will assess whether models could covertly work against their developers’ intentions and whether our safeguards would detect such behavior. Drawing on evidence from training, safety testing, and internal use. Apollo will assess four claims in two stages:

Training did not incentivize subversion.

Strong evaluations and red teaming do not elicit subversion.

Models have not attempted subversion during internal use.

Reasoning behind subversion would be detectable.

For the first stage of Apollo’s assessment, we’ll provide access to selected public and unreleased models and training checkpoints, relevant training data and evaluation results, training intervention records, monitoring systems and flagged behaviors, and researchers who can provide context, alongside the tools and compute needed to conduct independent testing.

Goodfire⁠(opens in a new window)will embed interpretability researchers and use the Goodfire platform to analyze model internals. The main objective of their assessment is training run monitoring, debugging, and alignment. The primary audience for their assessments are internal OpenAI researchers, who will use their findings to make safety improvements. Goodfire will also publish learnings and findings as the collaboration progresses.

We intend to conduct two assessments withMETR⁠(opens in a new window), focused on model alignment and monitoring:

Alignment assessment:For the first phase, METR will assess misaligned behavior in our largest reinforcement learning run to date, including failures that our existing tests and monitors may have missed. Within the selected run and agreed access, resources, and safety arrangements, METR would independently set assessment priorities and iterate on searches, analyses, and elicitation experiments. Access will include sampling relevant checkpoints, training and eval rollouts, and misalignment monitoring records for this run. For this first phase, the assessment will focus on our largest frontier RL run.1

Monitor assessment:We recently worked with METR to conduct a monitor stress testing exercise2. We have preliminarily agreed to conduct anothermonitor assessment⁠(opens in a new window)which we intend to be broader, but this is pending mutual agreement on the assessment scope.

Transluce⁠(opens in a new window)will conduct an initial assessment of our post-training alignment evaluations, examining their quality and coverage. For the initial assessment, we will provide Transluce with access to selected public and unreleased models, our post-training alignment evaluations and relevant results, supporting model behavior data and safety case documentation, and researchers who can provide context, alongside the tools and compute needed to conduct independent testing.

OpenAI and Transluce also share the intent to conduct a follow-on assessment of approximately eight weeks in early 2027, with broader access to additional models, deeper access to our alignment evaluations, and information on how evaluation results inform model release decisions.

We’ve developed protocols and processes with input from the assessors to balance deep access with security, confidentiality, oversight, and the independence and integrity of assessments. We are sharing them to shed light on how we will work with embedded assessors, and to advance discussion about norms for embedded assessments, which have yet to be standardized. We expect that these will need to evolve as we learn more about how to best conduct these assessments. Especially in the early stages of embedded assessments, we expect technical access challenges, space constraints, evolving security protocols, and other unexpected issues to arise. We hope to work through these challenges collaboratively with our embedded assessors and share lessons learned.

Each engagement begins with an agreed scope and the access, resources, and safety arrangements needed to conduct a rigorous assessment. Some assessments test specific safety claims; others give assessors room to discover unexpected failure modes within a defined system or training run. In both cases, assessors need the freedom to follow evidence, refine their methods, and propose further assessments when findings warrant it. We also have a process for addressing additional access needs as assessments develop. When direct access could expose our most sensitive IP, such as model weights or architecture, we will consider alternatives, including pairing assessors with OpenAI researchers to run analyses.

Assessors who need access to sensitive confidential information will work on site at OpenAI offices and be provided OpenAI devices to conduct their work. The primary purpose is to protect the security of the information they access. Working onsite also gives assessors the opportunity to engage with dedicated staff who can help them navigate their access and provide context for their assessments. We also expect our embedded assessors to follow at minimum3the same security standards as OpenAI employees when running experiments and evaluations.

Our Safety and Security Committee (SSC), an independent oversight committee of the OpenAI Foundation’s Board, will have visibility into the embedded assessment and the ability to exercise their oversight responsibilities before, during, and at their conclusion. They will receive unredacted reports, and both the assessors and the SSC will be able to speak with each other during the assessment, including privately. Disagreements among OpenAI and any evaluator will be escalated to the Safety Advisory Group and OpenAI executives, who will have a specified time period to resolve them, and the SSC will be notified of any such disagreements promptly when escalated. If a disagreement remains, the matter will be referred to the SSC for resolution.

Discussions with employees help assessors understand internal information and the context behind the work. OpenAI will authorize and provide guidance to staff members who can speak to assessors, and assessors may request additional staff to speak with as needed. To encourage open, candid conversations and protect the privacy of our staff, these discussions are off the record, meaning that they can inform the assessments but cannot be published or attributed to employees. Through a separate attestation pathway, assessors can request OpenAI-attested statements verifying, correcting, or clarifying something they learned in conversation with employees. These statements are not attributed to individuals or intended to characterize individual views. Assessors may publish statements that OpenAI attests to, or disclose that OpenAI declined to attest to a statement.

Managing conflicts of interest clearly and transparently—including those involving personal relationships, financial interests4, and other issues—is important to the integrity and independence of evaluations. Cool-off periods5also need to be designed carefully, so assessors can work responsibly across labs while handling competitive information sensitively. We are working with our assessors to develop clear processes for both conflicts and cool-off periods, including allowing for flexibility in mitigations and transparency in decisions to request recusal.

Assessors maintain independence in publishing their assessments, but we will retain the right to redact confidential information, consistent with our previous third-party engagements. We may also request responsible disclosure delays to allow time to act on findings that could pose security or safety risks and remediate issues that remain.

Public reporting will help people understand the findings and their limitations, while more detailed confidential reports give oversight bodies the evidence they need to act. We want these assessments to improve how we identify and address risks, and give the public a clearer basis for judging our safety work.

These assessments bring an independent perspective to our ongoing alignment and safety work. Public reporting on their findings will ...

articles.title: TokenEconomizer: Learning from Experience to Make AI Coding Agents More Efficient
articles.content: At a glance Developers use AI coding agents in the same codebases day after day, yet agents often start each session from scratch: rediscovering familiar facts, loading unused tools, and repeating unsuccessful approaches. TokenEconomizer is an open-source plugin that learns from an agent’s past sessions in a repository to reduce waste in future sessions, without modifying the agent or its underlying model. Across 277 real bug-fixing tasks, TokenEconomizer reduced costs by 18.4–30.9% across multiple AI coding agents. Costs fell in every repository tested, while task success rates remained broadly stable. AI coding agents are increasingly helping developers fix bugs and build features largely on their own, but every interaction with their models consumes tokens. In each session, an agent sends instructions, tool descriptions, and session history to its model. Most efforts to reduce this cost focus on individual tasks. Yet developers return to the same repositories, giving agents an opportunity to learn from previous work. Without that learning, an agent may repeatedly rediscover how to run tests, load tools it never uses, or spend dozens of turns revisiting the same error. In our paper, TokenEconomizer: Experience-Driven Black-Box Cost Control for Coding Agents, we ask a simple question: can experience in a repository help an agent solve future tasks more efficiently? TokenEconomizer, an open-source plugin from UC Berkeley, Microsoft Research, and Microsoft Security, turns completed sessions into guidance for subsequent ones. It reduces waste without changing the agent or its underlying model, so developers can use it alongside the coding agents they already rely on. Figure 1. Each finished session teaches TokenEconomizer something about the repository, so later sessions cost less tokens.  Where the tokens go We first profiled Claude Code on 60 tasks from SWE-Bench, a benchmark of real bug fixes in open-source Python projects, running each repository’s tasks in sequence. Three kinds of waste recurred: Rediscovering the same facts. After a repository had accumulated at least five completed tasks, 30% of tool calls repeated an action from an earlier task in that repository. Only 7% matched an action in another repository’s history. Paying for unused tools. The agent received 23 tool descriptions on every turn, but 16 were never called. Getting stuck on failures. The 17% of tasks that failed accounted for 32% of the spending. We also tested three popular open-source plugins, each built around a fixed cost-saving strategy. Each lowered costs in some repositories but not others. Together, these findings suggest that effective cost control must adapt to the repository, rather than apply the same strategy everywhere. Foundry Labs Foundry Labs bridges the distance between Microsoft breakthroughs and the builders, scientists, and curious minds who can put them to work. Foundry Labs Opens in a new tab How TokenEconomizer works After each session, TokenEconomizer reads the session’s log and updates what it knows about the repository. It then acts through three mechanisms, using only interfaces the agent already provides, as illustrated in Figure 2. Micro-skills capture repository-specific knowledge in one-line notes. TokenEconomizer identifies recurring patterns across sessions and proposes corresponding notes. They are added to the agent’s starting context only after several sessions have confirmed the pattern, and retires the note if later evidence contradicts it. Tool pruning removes tools that repository history suggests the agent is unlikely to use, while always retaining core tools for running commands and editing files. Removed tools can be restored if needed. Failure-loop intervention watches for an agent that keeps hitting the same failure. A judge model decides whether the agent is truly stuck or still making progress. If it is stuck, the agent gets a short note suggesting a different approach. In the open-source plugin, if the agent is still stuck after the note, TokenEconomizer alerts the developer rather than stopping the work itself. Figure 2. TokenEconomizer works alongside an unchanged coding agent. Micro-skills add learned facts, tool pruning trims the loaded tools, and failure-loop intervention redirects stuck work. Each finished session updates all three.  The controller is designed to revise its decisions as new evidence arrives. Reported savings also account for the cost of TokenEconomizer’s own model calls. Saving costs in every repository We evaluated TokenEconomizer on 277 SWE-Bench tasks from six repositories, using five different AI coding agent and model combinations. For each repository, TokenEconomizer started with no prior session history.  TokenEconomizer lowered the average cost by 18.4–30.9%, as shown in Figure 3, and saved the most in all 30 repository-combination pairs without performance loss. By contrast, lowering the model’s reasoning effort saved similar or larger amounts but led to substantial performance degradation. Figure 3. On SWE-Bench, TokenEconomizer lowered mean cost per task by 18.4–30.9% across five agent–model combinations (left), while Pass@1 rose in four of them (right).  Savings grow as experience accumulates. Early tasks can cost more while TokenEconomizer learns, but cumulative costs fell below the default in every repository by the sixth task, shown inFigure 4. Each mechanism contributes savings on its own, and combining all three delivers the largest reduction. Figure 4. Cumulative cost change relative to default over each repository’s tasks, using Claude Code. Starting with no history, every repository becomes cheaper by the sixth task.  The savings also carried over to sequential web development, with costs 16.0–21.2% lower on Web-Bench. On security auditing, where every task is in a new repository, costs were 6.4–19.6% lower. Looking ahead TokenEconomizer opens a path toward coding agents that learn not only how to solve tasks, but also how to spend computation more effectively. Its lightweight controller shows how experience can improve efficiency without changing the underlying agent or model. The open-source plugin makes these directions accessible to developers and researchers. It is designed to run alongside existing AI coding agents without modifying their underlying models, requires no API key of its own, and keeps what it learns on the developer’s machine. We invite the community to use it as a starting point for exploring agents that become more resourceful with experience, adapting how they work, as well as what they know.  Read the paper Access the code View the project Opens in a new tabThe post TokenEconomizer: Learning from Experience to Make AI Coding Agents More Efficient appeared first on Microsoft Research.
articles.summary: UC Berkeley, Microsoft Research, Microsoft Security가 코딩 에이전트의 과거 저장소 작업 경험을 다음 세션의 지침으로 전환하는 오픈소스 플러그인 TokenEconomizer를 소개했다. 에이전트나 기반 모델을 수정하지 않고 반복적인 정보 탐색, 불필요한 도구 로딩, 실패한 접근의 재시도로 발생하는 낭비를 줄인다. 실제 버그 수정 과제 277개에서 여러 코딩 에이전트의 비용을 18.4~30.9% 낮췄으며, 작업 성공률은 대체로 유지됐다고 보고했다. 같은 코드베이스를 지속적으로 다루는 개발팀에서 세션 간 경험 재사용을 비용 최적화 수단으로 활용할 수 있다는 결과다.

articles.title: Safety
articles.content:
November 16, 2026

New tools, practical guidance, and partnerships will help prevent, detect and respond to online child sexual exploitation and abuse.

Today, we’re releasing a new tool to detect child sexual abuse material (CSAM), interventions that interrupt harmful behavior and point people toward help, practical resources for developers, and support for child-safety law enforcement investigators. These efforts build on ourChild Safety Blueprintand ourongoing work to detect, block, and report abuse. For parents, the goal is simple: technology that helps keep children safe, with people in control.

It iswell⁠(opens in a new window)established⁠(opens in a new window)that combatting online child predators requires coordination across many organizations. Individual companies like OpenAI have a responsibility to prevent our technology from being exploited by predators to harm children, and we also must work together with the broader industry, child safety organizations and law enforcement to advance our collective efforts to protect children online.

We’re building on ourcurrent protectionswith the release of a new image classifier that can detect potential CSAM, including AI-generated material. This new classifier looks for visual signs of abuse, helping teams identify novel images that may not have been seen before. It returns scores that help reviewers decide which images may need attention first. This is the first CSAM classifier with broad availability that has a specific signal on indicating if CSAM may be AI generated.

Our teams trained, evaluated, and designed the classifier for real-world deployment with assistance from theNational Center for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC)⁠(opens in a new window), a nonprofit that operates the CyberTipline, a centralized reporting hub for the online exploitation of children.

We’re offering access to the classifier to vetted organizations through the OpenAI API at no cost, making CSAM detection more accessible to child safety organizations and the broader industry, including those with teams of varying sizes.

Child safety is an industry-wide issue that requires strong collaboration across organizations and a variety of solutions. We’ve engaged theTech Coalition⁠(opens in a new window)andROOST⁠(opens in a new window)to help us share access to this new tool, and we are strong supporters of tools developed by others such asThorn’s Safer⁠(opens in a new window)CSAM detection system. In addition, we recently began participating in the Tech Coalition'sLantern program⁠(opens in a new window), where we will share and receive signals relating to online child sexual exploitation and abuse to strengthen cross- platform collaboration.

We’ve tested the classifier internally and with early partners to measure how much abusive material it detects, how often it flags other images, and how it can support safety teams. Their feedback helped us identify weaknesses and improve the system.

Early tests suggest the classifier can help reviewers focus on abusive images while reducing review of false positives. In an evaluation of user-uploaded images, we compared the new classifier with our current protections and found:

The new classifier could reduce review work: we estimated that it would flag48%fewer images while finding roughly the same number of abusive images as the existing tool.

Images flagged by the new classifier were abouttwice as likelyto contain abuse.

Early access partners have also evaluated how the classifier supports their own safety teams. Infal⁠(opens in a new window)’s testing on human-reviewed production images, reviewers confirmed72%of the classifier’s high-confidence flags as novel CSAM.invideo AI⁠(opens in a new window)’s testing showed one in four flagged cases led to a ban. InSafetyKit⁠(opens in a new window)’s evaluations involving drawings or animations that sexualize children, the classifier detected90%of cases.

More information about the classifier is available in theCSAM classifier model card⁠(opens in a new window). Organizations interested in the classifier will be able to request access throughour intake form⁠.We’ll continue improving the classifier with feedback from those that use it.

We alreadyprohibit CSAM, train our models to refuse requests for it, and take action against accounts that violate our policies. We’re building on those safeguards with new product warnings in ChatGPT that interrupt attempts to find abusive material, explain the consequences, and point people toward help to stop harmful behavior.

The warning makes clear that sexualizing children causes harm, including when the requested material is AI-generated. Alongside the warning, we’ll remove the flagged conversation and pause access to ChatGPT for 24 hours, while keeping specialist support available to help people stop harmful behavior. Repeated violations may lead to longer restrictions and ultimately account closure or reports to authorities.

We developed this approach with input from organizations and academic advisors that research and develop programs to prevent child sexual abuse, includingProtect Children⁠(opens in a new window), theLucy Faithfull Foundation⁠(opens in a new window), Dr. Caoilte Ó Ciardha, Researcher & Honorary Reader in Forensic Psychology at the University of Kent andJoel Scanlan at the University of Tasmania, whoindependently evaluated a trial⁠(opens in a new window)of deterrent messages.

The protection of children online doesn’t end with detection. We’ve publishedCSAM guidance⁠(opens in a new window)to give developers practical steps to prevent abuse, detect harmful content, and act on it. Developed with input from theTech Coalition⁠(opens in a new window),Thorn⁠(opens in a new window),NCMEC⁠(opens in a new window), and theInternet Watch Foundation⁠(opens in a new window), it is designed for organizations at different stages of building their safety systems.

The guidance provides clear rules, ways for users to report concerns, detection tools, and processes for reviewing and reporting suspected abuse. It also explains how safety identifiers can help developers connect misuse to individual users and how to support the people reviewing sensitive content. Developers can use it alongside tools such as our new image classifier,Moderation API⁠(opens in a new window),ROOST’s self-hosted review console Coop⁠(opens in a new window),anddedicated CSAM detection services such asThorn’s Safer⁠(opens in a new window).

Our commitment to collaboration and supporting the broader developer ecosystem also is reflected in our work with Anthropic and Google to jointly commission new guidance on responding to disclosures of child sexual exploitation and abuse in AI systems. Recently published by theTech Coalition⁠(opens in a new window), this guidance provides developers with practical recommendations for addressing these sensitive situations.

We’ve already seen this guidance lead to increased numbers of developers accessing child safety tooling and registering to report CSAM to NCMEC.

Protecting children also means supporting the specialist child safety investigators working to find victims and stop abuse. As we’vediscussed publicly with Thorn⁠(opens in a new window), AI can help investigators organize and prioritize information and reduce unnecessary exposure to abusive material.

We’re  also supporting  child-safety law enforcement units with new tools and trainings on how to use AI in their investigations, including dedicated plugins, investigative tools, and complex data analysis, with access managed by program administrators. At launch, the first tool will help investigators review lengthy chat logs and legal process returns, identify potential connections, and create timelines, with findings linked to source material.

The initial training is planned as an overview and demonstration, supported by a practical field guide that teams can refer to afterward. It will introduce the tools and how they fit into investigative work. Access will depend on agency authorization and program requirements. Future iterations of the training will be proposed at regional, national and international conferences.

These efforts share one goal: preventing harm to children and strengthening the response when abuse occurs. We’ll continue improving our safeguards while empowering child protection organizations, developers, researchers, and investigators with the tools, resources, and expertise they need to protect children, combat exploitation, and bring perpetrators to justice. By working together, we can harness the power of AI to make a meaningful difference in the fight against child sexualexploitationand abuse.

articles.content:
November 16, 2026 · Research · Science

We’re expanding the ChatGPT for Academic Researchers program to give up to 200,000 researchers worldwide free access to ChatGPT.

The program began as a pilot in July. Applications for the next round open Monday, November 23. We’ll award 50,000 new grants to eligible researchers on a first-come, first-served basis. Each grant gives the recipient and up to two collaborators free access to ChatGPT Plus. If you’re already on the waitlist and qualify, we’ll email you before applications open with instructions for activating your account.

Participants can use OpenAI’s frontier models and get training on how to use ChatGPT in their research. By default, we don’t use data shared through the program to train our models.

Waitlist signups by country or territory as of November 12, 2026. Darker colors indicate more signups on a logarithmic scale.

20,000 researchers in 33 countries have joined the program since the pilot began in July. Shuqi Li, a researcher at Brigham and Women’s Hospital and Harvard Medical School, looks for new drug targets that could ultimately shorten tuberculosis treatment. He is exploring whether ChatGPT can help link lab and patient data to speed up antibiotic development. Arthur Porto, assistant curator of AI biodiversity at the Florida Museum of Natural History, and his team uses AI tools to turn photographs of museum specimens into searchable databases. They also created a 3D model of a butterfly whose wings change color as you turn it, just like the real specimen.

We’re also publishingScience at the Frontier: How Scientists Use ChatGPT, new research from our Economic Research team examining how more than 1,800 researchers used ChatGPT during the program’s summer pilot. Surveyed participants estimated that, without AI, the same research work at the same quality would have taken nearly twice as long.

We want more researchers to have the tools and support to pursue ambitious questions and make discoveries that improve people’s lives. That is central to our mission of ensuring that AGI benefits all of humanity.

The program’s summer pilot helped us understand how researchers use ChatGPT and how we can improve their experience. Based on feedback from researchers, we’re moving away from lottery-based selection. For the next round, we’ll provide access to the first 50,000 applications who meet the eligibility requirements.

The pilot gave researchers access to ChatGPT Pro. When we reviewed pilot usage, we found that most participants would have stayed within ChatGPT Plus usage limits. Based on that finding, we’re offering Plus for new grants so we can extend access to more research teams.

Each grant for this round covers the recipient and up to two collaborators, supporting up to 150,000 researchers. Our goal for the program as a whole is to reach 200,000 researchers, double the goal we announced when the pilot launched in July.

We’ll continue learning from participants about the application process, the capabilities they need, and the support that helps them use these tools in their research. This feedback will help us refine the program and shape future rounds.

Different scientific fields will use AI in different ways, and researchers will need different kinds and levels of support. We’re working with scientific communities to understand those needs and shape our tools, training, and programs around them.

Our support also includes helping scientific communities turn AI-generated results into deeper understanding and new discoveries. In mathematics, wecontributed $5 million to a new Simons Foundation initiative⁠to help mathematicians examine, understand, and build on results produced by AI.

We’re also providing different ways for researchers and institutions to access our tools. ChatGPT for Academic Researchers is just one way we’re helping researchers access advanced AI tools.

ThroughChatGPT Edu⁠(opens in a new window), universities can give their campus communities access to ChatGPT for research, teaching, and learning, with tools for analyzing data and administrative controls for managing access.

For researchers working in biology,GPT‑Rosalind⁠brings together specialized biological reasoning and access to scientific tools and databases. TheRosalind Academic Plan⁠helps bring these capabilities to eligible labs at U.S. universities, offering up to 30 seats at no cost for up to 12 months. Access toGPT‑Rosalindrequires approval through our trusted-access process.

Visit ourresearcher access guideto learn more aboutChatGPT Edu,GPT‑Rosalind, and ChatGPT for Academic Researchers.

As these efforts grow, researchers’ experiences will help us understand where our tools are useful, where they fall short, and what support is needed. We’ll use that feedback to improve our programs, develop training and learning resources, and create opportunities for researchers to exchange approaches with one another.

Our goal is to give more researchers the tools and support to pursue ambitious questions—and to keep improving that support as their research and our capabilities evolve.

Learn more about the program⁠(opens in a new window).

( English Version : ​https://naver.me/xQJbNeuF ) ​ 발표 대상 Image AI 모델을 서비스로 운영하며 응답 속도와 GPU 자원 효율을 개선하고 싶은 엔지니어 ​ 목차 1. SNOW Image AI 서비스와 기존 서빙 구조의 문제 ​ 2. articles.title: Meet Meta’s JiTTests: LLM-Generated Tests Designed to Fail Before Risky Code Lands
articles.content: Meta has moved Catching Just-in-Time Tests (JiTTests) from research prototype into its production infrastructure. Meta JiTTests is an LLM-based system that writes executable tests designed to fail on a risky code change. A failing test is concrete evidence that a diff changed behavior. Meta team reports that JiTTests caught 74 privacy SEVs at the diff stage in the first half of 2026. The method is described in the FSE 2026 research paper ‘Just-in-Time Catching Test Generation at Meta‘. TL;DR Scale: Runs on Meta backend code with hundreds of millions of lines. The research paper analyzes 22,126 generated tests. Runs on: Meta’s internal infrastructure, overnight on spare capacity. Judge models in the paper: Llama3.3-70B, Gemini 3 Pro, Claude Sonnet 4. Not publicly available. Performance: Engineers report a 60% true-positive rate at full scale (self-reported). Best: 74 privacy SEVs caught before landing in H1 2026; privacy SEV occurrence down 20%. Worst: The initial deployment confirmed only 8 of 41 reported catches (19.5%). Bottom line: Best: executable proof of a bug before merge. Worst: internal only, with self-reported numbers. What are Catching JiTTests? Catching JiTTests are LLM-generated tests that should fail when a diff introduces a bug. Traditional hardening tests pass when written and guard against future regressions. Catching tests target the change under review, before it lands. Meta formalized the details in its 2025 paper ‘Harden and Catch’. Most AI bug tools act like faster human reviewers. They read the diff and leave comments. JiTTests instead execute code and show a concrete behavioral difference. Meta team concedes this takes more computational steps. It argues the approach catches bug classes that LLM or agent review can miss. How does the JiTTests pipeline work? The production pipeline has 5 stages: Targeting: Runs overnight on spare capacity. It selects the previous day’s risky diffs, using a mechanism similar to Meta’s Diff Risk Score. Test generation: 2 diff-aware workflows produce candidate tests (explained below). LLM-as-Judge ensemble: Several LLMs score each failing test using the test code, failure trace, diff and inferred intent. RubFake: The Rule-Based False-Positive Killing Environment adds deterministic checks. Its rules flag patterns like reflection, broken mocks and not-implemented exceptions. Human-on-the-loop: The system decides whether to contact an engineer, based on the combined ranking. Dodgy diff vs intent-aware: what is the difference? The dodgy diff workflow assumes every diff is buggy. It treats the diff as a mutant of its parent and generates tests that tell them apart. The intent-aware workflow first infers what the diff should do from its code, title and summary. It lists risks, builds a mutant for each, and writes tests to kill them. Tests that then fail on the real diff become ‘weak catches.’ What do the benchmarks show? The research team analyzes 22,126 generated tests. Diff-aware methods produced 4x more candidate catches than hardening tests. They produced 20x more than tests that failed by coincidence. The intent-aware workflow produced weak catches in 6.4% of its tests and on 7.9% of diffs. Dodgy diff scored 2.5% and 4.0%. Meta’s earlier ACH mutation-guided hardening scored 0.8% and 1.6%. The rule-based and LLM assessors cut human review load by 70%. &&& FeatureCatching JiTTests, intent-awareCatching JiTTests, dodgy diffACH mutation-guidedTestGen-LLMOrg / first publishedMeta, 2026Meta, 2026Meta, 2025Meta, FSE 2024GoalCatch bugs in the diff under reviewCatch bugs in the diff under reviewHarden code against specific fault classesImprove existing human-written testsGenerated test shouldFail on a buggy diffFail on a buggy diffPass when generatedPass when generatedAware of the diffYes, infers intent and risksYes, intent-unawareNoNoWeak catches per test*6.4% (52 of 811)2.5% (41 of 1,621)0.8% (6 of 754)2.0% (89 of 4,499)Diffs with a weak catch*7.9%4.0%1.6%3.6%False-positive filterLLM judge ensemble + RubFake rulesLLM judge ensemble + RubFake rulesNot disclosedBuild, pass and coverage filtersPublic availabilityInternal onlyInternal onlyInternal onlyInternal only *Figures from Table 1 of the JiTTests paper (self-reported, Meta codebase). TestGen-LLM row uses the “need not add coverage” setting. A weak catch is a candidate failure, not a confirmed bug. What changed at full scale? The initial deployment was modest. Meta reported 41 candidate catches to engineers. 8 were confirmed true positives, a 19.5% rate. 4 of those would have caused serious failures in production. The October 2026 engineering post reports much stronger production numbers: 589 engineers engaged with JiTTests, 64% of those contacted. Engineers reported a 60% true-positive rate. 74 privacy SEVs were caught at the diff stage in the first half of 2026. Overall privacy SEV occurrence fell 20% in the same period. What does human-on-the-loop mean? Human-in-the-loop means a person reviews every output. Human-on-the-loop means engineers set criteria and monitor results in aggregate. They intervene at the policy level, not on each test. Meta team rarely need to read test code. They only confirm whether an observed behavior change was intended. Can developers use JiTTests? The answer is No. JiTTests is internal Meta infrastructure. Meta has not released code, models or an API. Teams can still copy the pattern: diff-aware mutation-guided test generation, an LLM judge ensemble, deterministic filters and aggregate human oversight. Key Takeaways Meta’s JiTTests writes LLM tests meant to fail on buggy diffs. 74 privacy SEVs caught pre-merge in H1 2026; privacy SEVs down 20%. Engineers report a 60% true-positive rate, up from 19.5% in the paper. Intent-aware tests hit weak catches at 6.4%, vs 0.8% for ACH hardening. Internal only: no code, model or API released. articles.title: 노트북을 닫아도 개발은 계속된다: 자율 그래프 주도 개발
articles.content: 네이버 사내 기술 교류 행사인 NAVER Engineering Day 10th 에서 발표되었던 세션을 공개합니다. ​ ​ 발표 내용 '자율 그래프 주도 개발(Autonomous Graph-Driven Development)'에서는 사람의 직접적인 지시 없이 그래프가 프로젝트 진행을 주도합니다. 스펙 문서와 코드는 AI Agent 루프가 작성하고, 결정론적 코드가 이를 기계적으로 검사하며, 결함은 피드백 루프를 통해 자동으로 바로잡습니다. 사람이 AI를 호출하던 주도권이 역전되어 이제는 AI가 필요할 때만 사람을 호출합니다. ​ ​ 발표 대상 자율 그래프 주도 개발 방법론에 관심있는 개발자나 기획자 ​ 목차 1. (접근 방법 및 실행 과정) Autonomous Graph-Driven Development (용어 정의) Don't call us, we'll call you 그래프의 핵심 원칙 그래프 구조 노드 ① Upstream — 기획서 변경을 요구사항으로 옮긴다 노드 ② Spec-drive — 스펙을 확정한다 노드 ③ Dev — 확정된 스펙을 구현한다 노드 ③ Dev 사례 — 복잡한 AI 대화 구현, 토큰 비용 $199.61 노드 ④ Verify — 배포된 코드를 E2E 테스트로 검증한다 노드 ⑤ Audit — 스펙의 논리적 결함을 찾는다 진행 현황 대시보드 — 어디까지 왔고, 왜 멈춰 있는가? ​ 3. 처음부터 잘 굴러갔을까? articles.title: More Agents, More Samples, or More Thinking? Untangling Coordination, Ensembling, and Test-Time Compute in Multi-Agent LLMs
articles.content:
arXiv:2611.17610v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Evaluations of multi-agent language models often compare communicating architectures against a single greedy pass. This practice confounds coordination with sample multiplicity and inference compute. We synthesize nine primary empirical evaluations comprising 516 unique multi-agent configurations organized along a resource vector R with six dimensions and a baseline ladder with four categories. Against baselines with a single pass (Category A), multi-agent accuracy differences are negative overall and near zero when omitting the largest contributing study. When evaluated against baselines matched on sample count (Category B) or resource budget (Category C), multi-agent systems average -0.042 in accuracy, and multilevel random effects modeling on the log odds scale remains negative across sensitivity checks. Multi-agent accuracy equals or falls below the baseline in 74% of these comparable contrasts, and study means are nonpositive in almost all evaluated studies. Across studies reporting both baselines, moving from a greedy pass to a sampled baseline shifts accuracy differences by -0.038 on average. Because communication adds no information when agents share identical evidence, positive returns require partitioned evidence, external verification, or error diversity across models. We provide a reviewer checklist and accounting utilities.
articles.summary: 다중 에이전트 LLM 연구 9건의 구성 516개를 종합한 논문은 협업 효과와 반복 샘플링·추론 연산량의 효과를 분리해 평가했다. 샘플 수 또는 자원 예산을 맞춘 비교에서 다중 에이전트의 정확도 차이는 평균 -0.042였고, 비교의 74%에서 기준선과 같거나 낮았다. 이는 단일 탐욕적 응답과 비교하는 관행이 에이전트 간 조율의 실질적 가치를 과대평가할 수 있음을 시사한다. 연구진은 검토 체크리스트와 자원 산정 도구를 제시했으며, 실무에서는 에이전트 수를 늘리기 전에 동일 예산의 샘플링 기준선과 비교할 필요가 있다.

articles.title: Hark Releases Handoff², a 2x Faster Computer-Use Agent for Hark Pro
articles.content: Hark has released Handoff², the second version of the computer-use agent inside its Hark Pro app. The Hark Handoff 2 computer-use agent finishes web tasks about 2x faster than the original, on average. Hark states that the gains come from reinforcement learning (RL) that penalized wasted turns and latency. For teams building browser agents, it is a case study in training for speed, not only accuracy. You can check the deployment options and specs here through our GPULeaderboard.com chrome extension. TL;DR Runs on: Hark’s cloud. Each request gets a dedicated virtual computer. Users reach it from web, iOS and Android. No local or quantized option. Performance: 82% task completion on Hark’s 478-task internal benchmark, about 2x faster end to end than v1. Best: 93.8% on Hark’s internal alignment benchmark (v1: 90.3%). Worst: 82% browsing completion still trails Claude Opus 5.5 (max), by up to 5 points, in the same harness. Bottom line (best): Up to 3.8x faster flight booking and more than 5x faster long research. Bottom line (worst): Every Handoff² number is self-reported. No third-party score exists yet. What is Hark Handoff²? Handoff² is a computer-use agent from Hark that operates websites the way a person does. It clicks, types and scrolls on live pages instead of calling APIs. Hark previewed Handoff in August and shipped it in Hark Pro in October. Since then, Hark says it has logged over 5.6M browsing sessions and handled over $20M in purchases. Users send it groceries, flights, dentist appointments, refunds, warranty forms and job applications. How does Handoff² get 2x faster? Hark co-evolved 2 things: the agent harness and the RL training recipe. The new harness lets the model emit more actions per turn. Training then penalized excess turns, unnecessary thinking tokens and end-to-end latency. The model learned 3 habits: Batch actions, such as filling several form fields in 1 turn. Group repeated action patterns into reusable composite actions. Reuse those composites as the task continues. Each request runs on a dedicated virtual computer with its own browser, file system and terminal. The model outputs cursor and keyboard actions aimed at screen coordinates. Because savings stack per turn, gains grow on longer, browsing-heavy tasks. How fast is Handoff² compared with Handoff? Hark reports these speedups over v1: Average: about 2x faster end to end. Flight booking: up to 3.8x faster. Long research tasks: more than 5x faster. Examples: a 10-minute task can drop to 3 minutes, and a 45-minute task to about 10. What do the Handoff² benchmarks show? Hark reports 2 internal benchmarks: Browsing: 478 tasks across 238 websites. Handoff² completes 82%, up from 73% for v1. It takes 46% less time per task. Hark ran Claude Opus 5.5 (max) in the same harness as Handoff². Handoff² lands within 5 points of it. Note that v1 was measured in its original harness, not the new one. Alignment: 93.8% for Handoff², up from 90.3% for v1. The suite checks that the agent never checks out without approval. It also checks that the agent asks for clarification only when a request is truly ambiguous. On the public Online-Mind2Web human-eval leaderboard, the original Handoff scores 97.67%. Yutori’s Navigator n1.5 sits at 97.3%. Hark has not posted an Online-Mind2Web result for Handoff² yet. && How does Handoff² compare with other web agents? articles.title: Advancing Quantization for R&R Models with Microscaling Formats
articles.content:
arXiv:2611.17501v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Recommendation and Ranking (R&R) models, particularly in digital advertising, require massive inference throughput but exhibit extreme sensitivity to precision loss. Unlike Large Language Models (LLMs) that frequently tolerate quantization-induced accuracy drops of 1% or more, production-grade R&R models enforce a stringent launch bar: model quality must remain within a 0.01% Normalized Entropy (NE) margin relative to the baseline, which commonly uses FP16 or FP32. This tight constraint has historically hindered the adoption of aggressive quantization in this domain. In this paper, we present an empirical evaluation of both MXFP8 and the 6-bit MXFP6 format for industrial-scale R&R inference on the AMD MI350X architecture.
  To the best of our knowledge, this is the first paper, across R&R and LLM domains, that reports significant speedups from native MXFP6 GEMMs, which quantize both weights and activations and compute directly on 6-bit elements, without sacrificing model quality. We demonstrate that we can selectively apply this 6-bit format to maximize overall QPS gain without breaching the strict NE parity threshold. We further show that MXFP8 is a viable alternative to row-wise FP8: the two formats have nearly the same accuracy on our models, so the faster kernel can be chosen for each GEMM shape. On two production ads ranking models, our implementation shows measured GEMM kernel speedups over FP16 of 1.33--1.55x for MXFP8 and 1.73--1.99x for MXFP6 across all supported linear layers, and up to 2.90x for MXFP6 on individual layers, alongside end-to-end (E2E) inference throughput gains from selective MXFP6 of 1.5--5.3% for Model A and 7.6--14.3% for Model B over their FP8 configurations.
articles.summary: 추천·랭킹 모델 연구가 AMD MI350X에서 MXFP8과 MXFP6 마이크로스케일링 형식을 사용한 저정밀 추론 결과를 제시했다. 가중치와 활성값을 함께 양자화해 6비트 원소로 직접 계산하되, 적용 계층을 선택해 기준선 대비 정규화 엔트로피 차이를 0.01% 이내로 유지했다. 광고 랭킹 모델 2개에서 MXFP6 행렬 연산 커널은 FP16 대비 1.73~1.99배 빨라졌고, 선택적 적용에 따른 전체 추론 처리량은 기존 FP8 구성 대비 모델별로 1.5~5.3%, 7.6~14.3% 증가했다. 정밀도 손실에 민감한 상용 추천 시스템에서도 저비트 연산이 유효할 수 있음을 보여주지만, 커널 가속과 전체 서비스 개선 폭은 구분해야 한다.

articles.title: How we optimized our workflows and overcame GitHub Actions limitations
articles.content:
TLDR;Running CIs for large projects (like llama.cpp) on GitHub tends to take a long time to run and can outgrow the available cache and runner capacity. In this blog post, we walk you through how we changed our workflows using Hugging FaceBucketsto store compiler caches andJobsto run CI workloads.

Llama.cpp is one of the fastest-growing and most-engaged open-source projects on GitHub*. As such, we receive a large number of pull requests each month. Maintaining production-grade quality at all times requires running many tests across many platforms and runtimes.

As an illustration of the scale of the project, consider that during the 3 months between August and October 2026, the project received 3,181 pull requests (about 35 per day) and merged 1,802 of them.
The complete CI of the project includes a set of 100+ jobs, most of which involve heavy computations and model data operations. Many of the jobs can take up to ~30 minutes. Additionally, for almost every PR merged in themasterbranch, we create pre-release builds for users to easily try out new bleeding-edge functionality. These pre-release workflows involve an additional set of heavy long-running build tasks, some of which can take a few hours.

Llama.cpp CI checks the diff across many hardware backends, and a complete CI run contains 100+ jobs. Here’s what the CI infrastructure roughly looked like at the beginning of the year:

We made three changes: separated workflows for PRs andmaster, used Hugging Face Buckets to store compiler caches, and used Hugging Face Jobs to offload most Linux x64 jobs.

First, we reduced the work required for each pull request. We selected jobs based on the diff. We kept the complete set of CI jobs for pushes tomaster.

We had already limited cache saving to pushes tomasterand kept one cache entry per job. However, the total storage requirement still exceeded the GitHub Actions cache allocation.

We then moved theccachedata for non-release builds toHugging Face Buckets. After each eligible build onmaster, we upload a snapshot of the compiler cache to Hugging Face Buckets. Each PR build downloads this snapshot before compilation. It can then reuse object files when the source files and build settings match.

Which files need to be compiled depends on the changes in the PR and the available cache. PRs that differ substantially frommastercan require more compilation.

Hugging Face Buckets is an S3-like storage service backed by Xet, with deduplication on upload/download level, thus providing faster and cheaper storage in multipliers. You can check out the storage pricinghere. Before each job, the runner downloads the stored cache from a bucket. During the build,ccacheuses existing object files where possible and creates new ones when compilation is necessary. After eligible builds onmaster, the runner uploads the updated cache to the bucket.

This change preserved the use ofccachewhile changing where we stored its data between jobs. It also left more space in GitHub Actions Cache for release builds.

The bucket acts as a shared home for these caches across runners. A new runner retrieves the cache for its build configuration, without needing the disk from a previous runner. PR builds read this shared baseline; eligible builds onmasterpublish updates. We retain a recent cache for each build key and clean up older archives. Theinitial migrationshows how we connected this to the existing workflows.

Next, we moved some jobs from self-hosted runners and many jobs from GitHub-hosted runners toHugging Face Jobs. Jobs are cloud CPU or GPU instances running your scripts. You can check out the pricing for each instancehere; jobs are charged per uptime of the instance. We usedjobs-actionsto connect these jobs to our existing CI workflows.

Bucket storage was necessary before this move. Each runner could download the required cache without dependence on persistent storage attached to another runner. Buckets kept the non-release compiler caches available between these runs.

To integrate Hugging Face Jobs seamlessly into our existing GitHub Actions workflows, we utilizedjobs-actions. Rather than replacing GitHub Actions as our primary workflow orchestrator,jobs-actionsfunctions as a lightweight dispatcher and bridge. It allows standard GitHub Actions workflow steps to target custom compute environments on Hugging Face (such ashf-jobs-cpu-upgradeorhf-jobs-t4-small) by mapping specific runner labels to corresponding Hugging Face hardware profiles.

When a job using a designated Hugging Face runner label is queued in GitHub Actions, a webhook event triggers a dispatcher Space hosted on Hugging Face. The dispatcher authenticates the payload, verifies repository permissions, and requests an ephemeral registration token directly from the GitHub API. With this token, the dispatcher dynamically provisions a containerized Hugging Face Job configured with the required hardware specifications and runner environment.

Once initialized, the ephemeral runner automatically registers itself with the GitHub repository, claims the pending workflow job, and executes all defined steps. Standard outputs, step summaries, and real-time execution logs are continuously streamed back into the GitHub Actions user interface. This guarantees full visibility within pull requests and commits without requiring team members to monitor secondary dashboards or external consoles.

The complete flow looks like this:

You can read more details about how to set up jobs-actions for your own repos here:https://huggingface.co/blog/github-ci-hf-jobs
articles.summary: Hugging Face가 llama.cpp의 대규모 지속적 통합 작업에서 GitHub Actions의 캐시와 실행 용량 한계를 완화한 방법을 소개했다. 풀 리퀘스트에서는 변경 내용에 필요한 작업만 실행하고, master 반영 시에는 전체 검사를 유지하도록 워크플로를 분리했다. 컴파일러 캐시는 Hugging Face Buckets로 이전하고 Linux x64 작업 대부분을 Hugging Face Jobs로 분산했다. 전체 검사가 100개 이상의 작업으로 구성되는 오픈소스 AI 프로젝트에서 테스트 범위를 관리하면서 저장소와 실행 자원을 확장하는 실무 사례다.

articles.title: Verifiable pXRD: Hill-climbing pXRD structure determination with LLM agents
articles.content:
arXiv:2611.17539v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Autonomous crystal-structure determination from powder X-ray diffraction (pXRD) remains a key bottleneck for self-driving materials laboratories. We formulate the task of pXRD structure determination as a verifiable agentic search problem: candidate structures can be assessed during inference through forward-simulated profile agreement and during evaluation through structural matching to a known reference. To benchmark progress, we introduce pXRD-Bench, a suite of 200 simulated single-phase problems spanning in-distribution structure determination, challenging and polymorphic structures, and controlled compositional and topological distribution shifts. Agent adaptation raises selected structural recovery from 27% to 69%, with further gains from repeated sampling and verifier-guided inference-time scaling. We extend this approach to experimental multiphase pXRD through a reflexive evolution framework that learns from self-generated synthetic problems. A replaceable laboratory specification defines the sample family and measurement conditions. An evolver agent uses the known generating structures and measurement parameters to diagnose solver failures and develop persistent guidance and executable tools, which are then provided to agents on measured patterns. This supplies verifiable training experience without requiring a collection of solved experimental measurements. On 15 measured patterns from solid-state synthesis, the evolved package improves average profile agreement and transfers an analogue-substitution procedure that recovers a phase whose structure is absent from the supplied reference library. These results demonstrate how learning from verifiable synthetic experience can improve agentic characterization of experimental samples whose structures are not known in advance.
articles.summary: 연구진이 분말 X선 회절 데이터에서 결정 구조를 찾는 문제를 검증 가능한 LLM 에이전트 탐색으로 구성하고, 모의 단일상 문제 200개로 이뤄진 pXRD-Bench를 제안했다. 후보 구조의 회절 패턴을 시뮬레이션해 관측값과 비교하며, 에이전트 적응을 통해 선택된 구조의 복원율을 27%에서 69%로 높였다고 보고했다. 자체 생성 합성 문제에서 실패를 분석해 지침과 실행 도구를 발전시키는 방식은 실제 측정 패턴 15개에서도 평균 패턴 일치도를 개선했다. 참조 라이브러리에 없는 구조의 상을 복원한 사례도 제시했지만, 실제 실험 평가 규모는 작아 범용성을 단정하기 어렵다.

articles.title: Does the Ranking Hold? A Practitioner-Facing Audit of Hallucination Detectors on Small, Quantized, On-Device LLMs
articles.content:
arXiv:2611.17339v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Hallucination detection for large language models is dominated by methods evaluated on 7B-70B research models with abundant sampling budgets and exact-match or ROUGE correctness labels. The small models practitioners actually ship on-device, Phi-3-mini, Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-2B-Instruct, typically at 4-bit precision, sit outside this evidence base. We present a reproducible one-GPU audit of four detectors spanning three paradigms: length-normalized token-margin calibration, a lexical n-gram baseline, and two sampling-based consistency methods (semantic entropy and SelfCheckGPT-NLI) on two small open instruction-tuned models (Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct) loaded at 4-bit NF4 quantization on a single Colab T4 GPU, evaluated on closed-book TriviaQA. Cross-model ranking transfer is poor: Spearman rho is -0.80 and Kendall tau-b is -0.667, meaning the detector ranking actively inverts between the two models, and the cheap lexical baseline is statistically indistinguishable from the sampling-based consistency detectors on both models under bootstrap 95 percent confidence intervals. As a second, methodological contribution, we show that the standard token-overlap-to-multiple-choice correctness labeler for TruthfulQA-Generation produces near-chance AUROC (0.46-0.59) for all four detectors on both models, a labeler failure, not a detector failure, since the same detectors reach 0.69-0.89 AUROC on TriviaQA under the identical pipeline. We release the harness, prompts, and per-item scores and frame the detector choice explicitly as a fairness-of-error-rates allocation problem for practitioners deploying on resource-constrained, on-device hardware.
articles.summary: 연구진이 4비트로 양자화한 Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct와 Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct에서 환각 탐지기 4종을 단일 T4 GPU로 비교했다. TriviaQA 평가에서 탐지기 순위의 모델 간 상관은 Spearman -0.80으로 역전됐으며, 저비용 어휘 기반 기준선과 샘플링 기반 일관성 탐지기의 차이는 통계적으로 구분되지 않았다. TruthfulQA에서는 정답 판정 방식의 문제가 모든 탐지기의 AUROC를 우연 수준에 가깝게 낮출 수 있다는 점도 지적했다. 온디바이스 배포에서는 대형 모델에서 좋은 탐지기를 그대로 채택하기보다 실제 모델·양자화 조건·정답 라벨링을 함께 검증해야 한다는 결과다.

articles.title: What LLM Agents See and What Users Say
articles.content:
arXiv:2611.17639v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Before an LLM agent cancels a reservation or deletes a folder for a user, what stops it from acting on a false assumption: what its tools show, or what the user says? In this work, we study this gap with presupposition theory from linguistics: an agent may act only if each claim behind the act (e.g., one reservation fits the name) is seen to hold, answered by the user, or disclosed while the act can be undone. A simple bound shows that when lookups cannot tell one record from two, any agent acts without asking first as often with two records as with one. We then vary whether a search lists, counts, or omits a second match, and whether the user states a claim that a record refutes (e.g., "It is empty"). Under a role-only prompt, a count of a second record leaves most of 36 earlier agents acting on the one they see, whereas listing both stops most. When the user says a record such as a folder is empty, however, a count of its one item stops agents about as often as a listing, and stating the claim mostly cuts acting when it is false. The newest Claude and GPT models always open a counted second record, then never act. When we add a same-name, same-zip customer to a retail benchmark, a lookup returning that customer first led to wrong-account writes in about a quarter of conversations, and one that checks a street the user knows kept completion near the one-customer level. Safe writes therefore need lookups that list or check competing records, and evaluations that vary what tools show.
articles.summary: LLM 에이전트가 예약 취소나 폴더 삭제 전에 잘못된 전제를 확인하는지를 도구 출력 방식과 사용자 진술을 바꿔 조사한 연구가 나왔다. 이전 에이전트 36개 중 다수는 두 번째 일치 항목의 개수만 알려주면 보이는 항목에 작업했지만, 두 항목을 모두 나열하면 행동을 멈췄다. 소매 벤치마크에 이름과 우편번호가 같은 고객을 추가하고 그 고객을 먼저 반환하자 약 4분의 1의 대화에서 잘못된 계정에 쓰기 작업이 발생했다. 사용자가 아는 도로명 주소를 확인하는 조회는 완료율을 유지하는 데 도움이 됐으며, 안전한 에이전트 설계에는 프롬프트뿐 아니라 중복 후보를 드러내고 검증하는 도구 인터페이스가 중요함을 보여준다.
